theme: More, less, and the glass that lies

activities.title: Big is not the same as more
activities.intro: Some of these things are big and some are little. Big and more are not the same thing at all. Count both sides before you tap.
activities.offScreen: Go and find one big thing, and then a handful of little things. Hold them up and tell a grown-up which one is more, and how you know.

rounds.prompt: One big block over here, and some little blocks over there. Tap the side that has more blocks.
One big cup, and some little cups. Count the little ones out loud, then tap the side that has more cups.
Big stones on this side and little stones on that side. Count them both. Tap the side that has more stones.
Little stars here and big stars there. Count them both. This time tap the side that has fewer stars.

activities.title: More than this one
activities.intro: The grey card up at the top is not for tapping. It is there for you to count. Count the grey card first, then count each pile, then tap the one the question asks for.
activities.offScreen: Put four spoons on the table and count them. Now go and find a pile of something with more than four in it, and bring it back to show somebody.

rounds.prompt: The grey card shows four stones. Count each blue pile. Tap the pile that has more stones than the grey card.
The grey card shows six cups. Count each purple pile. Tap the pile that has fewer cups than the grey card.
The grey card shows five coins. These piles are close together, so count carefully. Tap the pile that has more coins than the grey card.
The grey card shows seven blocks. Tap the pile that has exactly the same number of blocks as the grey card, not more and not fewer.

activities.title: Fewest first
activities.intro: Three piles this time. Count all three, then tap them in order, the pile with the fewest things first and the biggest pile last.
activities.offScreen: Make three piles of your toys, a little one, a middle one and a big one. Line them up fewest first, then tell a grown-up which pile is in the middle.

rounds.prompt: Three piles of cups. Count them all, then tap them in order with the fewest first.
Three piles of stones. Count them all, then tap them in order with the fewest first.
Three piles of coins. These ones are close, so count each pile twice. Then tap them in order with the fewest first.
Three piles of blocks, and one of them is a whole ten. Count them all, then tap them in order with the fewest first.

parentCard.title: The pouring test on the porch
steps: Take two glasses out to the porch, one tall and thin and one short and wide, with a jug of water and a towel. Let them carry the jug, and let some of it spill.

Fill the short wide glass first, as full as they like, and ask them to look at it hard. Then ask before anything moves: if we pour this into the tall skinny one, will it be more water, less water, or the same water? Take their answer as it comes and do not correct it.

Pour it, and let them watch the water climb high up the tall glass. Ask again: is it more now? Most children this age say yes here, and that is the whole point of the afternoon, so let the yes stand and say nothing clever.

Now let them pour it back, and across again, two or three times, doing all the pouring themselves. Somewhere in the middle ask the why question and then wait as long as it takes: why does the tall glass make it look like more?

Finish with the walking part. Go round the garden hunting for pairs where one thing looks bigger but the other one is more: a big stone against a handful of pebbles, one tall flower against a low bunch of them. They decide each pair and say why.
notice: When the water goes back into the wide glass, do they change their mind, or do they stay with what their eyes told them? Both are completely normal at this age.
Do they reach for counting anywhere, cupfuls or pours or gulps, or are they only ever looking?
When you ask why the tall glass fools us, do they talk about the water or about the glass?
